units.title: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards and math, code and structured tasks
outcomes: Explain why RLVR replaces a learned reward model with a verification function on math, code and structured tasks, and state what the verifier checks.
Build a boxed-answer and unit-test reward on fixed completions, with all-pass gating and a stated partial-credit rule.
Compute group-relative advantages from fixed rollout rewards with a stated standard-deviation convention.
units.why: Verifiable tasks let RL train on correctness instead of preference. The reward is code, so its gating and format rules decide what the policy learns.

next.note: Isolate the verifier and hold out tests before trusting the reward.
Control for sampling and selection before calling a gain learned.

study.title: Tulu 3 RLVR stage
study.locator: Section 6, RLVR Recipe and Analyses, arXiv:2411.15124v5: SFT then DPO then RLVR with verifiable math and constraint rewards; read the recipe and infrastructure, not the 8B and 70B numbers as targets

focus: RLVR pays 1 on verified correct else 0, with all-pass gating for tests. Partial credit is a different estimand, so state which rule is used.
Boxed format is part of the reward when `fallback=None`. Track format and correctness rewards as separate terms.
The MATH-500 exclusion prevents train-test leakage. A verifier does not fix contaminated data.
RLVR revisits the same prompts for hundreds of epochs while SFT uses 1 or 2. Length growth is a side effect, not proof of reasoning.
units.reproduce: From a blank file, score 5 fixed math completions with boxed extraction plus `grade_answer` and 3 fixed code completions with all-pass unit-test gating. Then compute advantages for rewards `[1.0, 1.0, 0.0, 0.0]` with mean subtraction and unbiased `torch.std` plus `1e-4` to get `[0.8659, 0.8659, -0.8659, -0.8659]`.
traps: Treating a longer trace as a better trace. Length rises under RLVR by default, so check correctness per token budget.
Taking the first boxed answer or a number-regex fallback as correct. The book takes the last boxed answer and requires the box when `fallback=None`.
Porting Listing 6.8 to NumPy with default `ddof=0` and expecting 0.8659. NumPy gives 1.0 because the book uses unbiased `torch.std`.

selfTest.q: A fib solution passes 2 of 3 asserts under all-pass gating. What reward does it get?
selfTest.a: 0. Only all-pass gives 1. Proportional credit is a separate rule with its own gradient.

selfTest.q: Why does the book set `fallback=None` in `reward_rlvr`?
selfTest.a: A correct number outside a box then scores 0. Format compliance becomes part of the reward.

selfTest.q: Compute advantages for rewards `[1.0, 1.0, 0.0, 0.0]` with unbiased standard deviation plus `1e-4`.
selfTest.a: Mean 0.5 and standard deviation about 0.5774 give `[0.8659, 0.8659, -0.8659, -0.8659]`.

selfTest.q: Why does RLVR run hundreds of epochs over the same prompts while SFT uses 1 or 2?
selfTest.a: RLVR reinforces rare correct behaviors into robust ones by revisiting. SFT matches completions. Gains must still be checked on held-out prompts.

units.title: Verifier isolation, hidden tests and sparse outcome credit
outcomes: Separate visible verifier tests from hidden tests and state what each set can and cannot prove.
Implement all-pass gating and partial credit on fixed code outputs and show how the rule changes the update.
Explain sparse terminal credit with a discounted-return example and why the final score cannot name the first error.
units.why: The policy optimizes exactly what the verifier pays for. Isolation and scoring rules decide whether higher reward means solved or means gamed.

next.note: Add step feedback only after terminal credit is sound.
Attack the verifier before trusting its score.

study.title: R1-Zero rule-based rewards
study.locator: Sections 2 and 3, arXiv:2501.12948v2: R1-Zero rule-based accuracy plus format rewards and language-consistency rewards for math, code and logic; read the pipeline as a claim map, not as a run target

study.title: Countdown verifier datasets and scoring
study.locator: Section 1.2.4 verifier-based datasets for RLOO only, Section 1.3.3 rule-based verifier reward, Section 1.4 evaluation with `evaluation/countdown.py` checking format plus arithmetic with multiple samples per prompt and average score plus pass at K

focus: The verifier runs outside the policy with frozen tests. Visible tests teach format while hidden tests decide the score.
All-pass gating pays 1 only when every assert passes. Partial credit pays a per-test share on the same outputs.
Terminal credit gives one reward to the whole trace. Discounted return with \(G_t = \gamma^{T-t}\) shrinks early weight with distance, which misattributes early defining errors.
Format rewards stabilize parsing but can be hacked into fluent wrong answers. Track format and accuracy separately.
units.reproduce: From a blank file, score 3 fixed code outputs under all-pass gating and under proportional partial credit and show one case where they disagree. Then compute returns for \(r_T = 1\) with \(\gamma = 0.9\) at 8, 4, 3 and 1 steps from the end to get 0.43, 0.66, 0.73 and 0.90.
traps: Letting the policy read verifier code or hidden tests during training. That turns evaluation into training data.
Averaging format and accuracy into one scalar. A format fix can mask an accuracy drop.
Treating discounted return as error location. It weights by distance, not by responsibility.

selfTest.q: A solution passes 2 of 3 asserts. What do all-pass and proportional rules pay?
selfTest.a: 0 and about 0.67. Same outputs give different updates.

selfTest.q: Why keep hidden tests the policy never sees?
selfTest.a: Visible tests teach format while hidden tests check generalization. A policy that saw them could memorize answers.

selfTest.q: With only \(r_T = 1\) and \(\gamma = 0.9\), what credit does a step 8 positions back get?
selfTest.a: About 0.43. That is distance discounting, not causal credit.

selfTest.q: A trace ends right but step 6 has a missing square. What does the outcome reward reinforce?
selfTest.a: The whole trace including step 6. That is the sparse-credit problem.

units.title: Process rewards, step credit and reasoning traces versus observable answers
outcomes: Contrast outcome and process rewards by input, data format and training signal, and state when steps are worth the cost.
Explain why hidden thinking tokens are not evidence of reasoning, and name the observable check that would support a claim.
Describe how PRM scores enter training per step without becoming per-token correctness labels.
units.why: One final score cannot say which step failed. Step feedback helps only when steps have stable meaning and errors propagate.

next.note: Use step scores to stop bad paths early at inference.
Distill only traces whose answers verify.

study.title: Format rewards and think tokens
study.locator: Chapter 7, Section 7.6, printed pp.256-266: `<think>` format reward, training a model to emit think tokens, and length and format incentives as separate terms

focus: ORM maps a prompt plus full response to one scalar. PRM adds a step index and scores that step.
R1-Zero develops longer self-checking traces from rule-based accuracy plus format rewards alone. Process labels are not required.
Thinking tokens are sampled text, not observed cognition. Only the extracted answer and its checks carry the claim.
A PRM score attaches per step or per token group. Sharing a score across tokens in a step is convention, not proof.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write \(\text{ORM}(q,o)\) and \(\text{PRM}(q,o,i)\) with their data tuples, and retell the square-root-of-2 story: outcome reward 1 for the whole trace despite the step-6 error. Then state the three checks for buying PRM: stable step meaning, propagating errors, and a judge more reliable than the generator.
traps: Calling a longer thinking trace proof of reasoning. Length and self-check phrases can grow while the answer stays wrong.
Training on step labels and claiming broad generality. Labels, candidate generator and rerank setup bound the claim.
Treating a PRM step score as a token correctness certificate. Tokens in one step share the score by convention.

selfTest.q: What are the inputs and data rows for ORM versus PRM?
selfTest.a: ORM takes prompt plus full response with final correctness. PRM adds a step index with step correctness.

selfTest.q: Why did the square-root-of-2 trace get reward 1 despite the step-6 error?
selfTest.a: The outcome verifier checks only the conclusion, so the whole trace shares the reward.

selfTest.q: When is PRM worth its annotation and compute cost?
selfTest.a: Steps have stable meaning, errors propagate and waste budget, and the step judge beats the generator. Short answers with cheap resampling usually fail this test.

selfTest.q: Are hidden thinking tokens evidence of how the model reasoned?
selfTest.a: No. They are generated text. Evidence comes from the extracted answer, verifier checks and held-out behavior.

units.title: Inference-time search, self-consistency and train-time versus test-time compute
outcomes: Run greedy, self-consistency and a small search on fixed prompts and report accuracy per token budget.
Explain why a reasoning gain can come from sampling, search or longer outputs rather than a better policy.
Design a compute-matched comparison that separates learned behavior from inference-time selection.
units.why: More samples or deeper search raise scores without changing weights. A learning claim must survive a matched inference budget.

next.note: Distill the searched behavior only after the selection effect is measured.
Check the search gain on held-out tasks before reporting it.

study.title: Self-consistency over sampled reasoning paths
study.locator: Chapter 4, Section 4.6, printed pp.127-135: sampling diverse completions with temperature and top-p, then majority vote over extracted answers

study.title: Beam search, tree search and answer aggregation
study.locator: Sections 2 and 3: fixed-width beam expansion with parallel paths, tree-of-thought backtracking, MCTS selection with `UCB(n)` worked example at parent 100 giving 1.23, 1.25 and 1.96; cost table from greedy 1 call to tree growth `B^D` (page read 2026-10-14)
study.depth: Treat the 24-Game GPT-4 percentages as an author-reported illustration, not as your target. Recompute the UCB numbers by hand.

focus: Self-consistency votes over answers, not over traces. Shared wrong prefixes can win the vote.
Search reuses prefixes and prunes bad paths early. Best-of-N pays full cost per sample with no reuse.
Report tokens, verifier calls and latency beside accuracy. A higher score at 10 times the tokens is a budget effect until proven otherwise.
RLVR training often lengthens outputs by default. Separate length growth from policy improvement.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, recompute the three UCB values for parent visits 100 with `c = 1.414`: child A with `Q = 0.8` and `N = 50` gives 1.23, child B with 0.7 and 30 gives 1.25, child C with 0.6 and 5 gives 1.96. Then state the cost order: greedy 1 call, best-of-N N calls, beam `K` times depth, tree `B^D`.
traps: Comparing a searched score against a greedy baseline and calling the gap learned. Match samples and tokens first.
Letting the vote see the test labels through prompt tuning. Fix prompts before sampling.
Reading parallel breadth as free speedup. It shortens waiting time with more hardware but not total compute.

selfTest.q: Why does best-of-N waste compute relative to beam search on shared prefixes?
selfTest.a: Best-of-N regenerates each sample from scratch. Beam search expands shared prefixes once and scores continuations.

selfTest.q: Child C has the lowest Q but the highest UCB in Reproduce. Why?
selfTest.a: Its visit count 5 is small, so the exploration bonus dominates. UCB picks it to reduce uncertainty.

selfTest.q: A distilled model matches the searched teacher. Is that proof the student reasons?
selfTest.a: No. It proves the student imitates selected outputs. Test the student greedy on held-out tasks at a fixed token budget.

selfTest.q: What must a train-versus-test compute comparison fix?
selfTest.a: Prompts, samples per prompt, tokens per sample, verifier calls and decoding. Then attribute the remaining gap.

units.title: Rejection fine-tuning, rollout and on-policy distillation and reasoning-length control
outcomes: Run a generate, filter by correctness and fine-tune loop on fixed rollouts and state how it differs from a policy gradient.
Contrast offline sequence distillation with on-policy distillation by sampling distribution and KL direction.
Control reasoning length with budgets and invalid-trace handling, and report length beside accuracy.
units.why: Filtered rollouts teach format and skill without RL. Distillation copies selected behavior, so its filters and length rules are the method.

next.note: Extend filtered traces to multi-turn tool trajectories.
Treat length as a compute budget in curricula and accounting.

study.title: From offline to on-policy teacher-student distillation
study.locator: The Path to On-Policy, Teacher-Student Distillation: sequence-level distillation with point-mass approximation, offline forward KL versus on-policy reverse KL, exposure bias with \(O(\epsilon L^2)\) compounding, multi-teacher mixture weights (page read 2026-10-14)

study.title: Distilling reasoning into Qwen3 0.6B
study.locator: Chapter 8, Sections 8.2 to 8.7, printed pp.271-295: DeepSeek-R1 teacher traces with `<think>` formatting, filtering 12000 to 6695 at 2048 tokens, train 6670 with val 25, answer-only cross-entropy 1.68; teacher 90.6 percent versus base 15.2 percent on MATH-500
study.depth: Run the 10-example demo on CPU or your GPU first. Use `max_len` 1024 or 512 for the full run on a small GPU.

focus: STaR filters rollouts by correctness and fine-tunes with cross-entropy. No importance ratio or advantage enters.
Offline distillation matches the teacher on teacher prefixes with forward KL. On-policy distillation samples student prefixes with reverse KL.
Answer-only loss trains teacher answer tokens, not prompt tokens. Length filtering at 2048 decides feasibility on small hardware.
Invalid traces need an explicit policy: drop, finish with 0, or repair. Each choice changes the estimand.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, write the STaR loop in three lines: generate rationales, keep correct ones, fine-tune. Then state the distillation numbers: 12000 built, 5305 removed at 2048, train 6670 with val 25, answer-only loss 1.68, teacher 90.6 percent on the distill set.
traps: Calling rejection fine-tuning RL. It has no policy gradient, only filtered supervised updates.
Sharing a tokenizer assumption silently. Per-token teacher feedback needs matching vocabularies.
Reporting distilled accuracy without length. A longer student can win by budget, not by skill.

selfTest.q: How does STaR differ from a GRPO update on the same rollouts?
selfTest.a: STaR keeps correct traces and fine-tunes with cross-entropy. GRPO computes group advantages and takes a policy gradient step with ratios.

selfTest.q: What changes between offline and on-policy distillation?
selfTest.a: The sampling distribution and KL direction. Offline uses teacher prefixes with forward KL. On-policy uses student prefixes with reverse KL.

selfTest.q: Why filter at 2048 tokens and keep val at 25?
selfTest.a: Length decides memory feasibility: 5305 of 12000 exceed 2048. A tiny val set keeps the loop fast; MATH-500 is the real check.

selfTest.q: A trace has no boxed answer. What are the three handling options?
selfTest.a: Drop it, keep it with reward 0, or repair the format. Each changes what the update estimates.

Implement a multi-turn rollout loop with an action mask that keeps observation tokens out of the loss.
Explain trajectory-level rewards with delayed credit and why every step shares one outcome by default.
units.why: Tool answers arrive over turns, but the reward arrives at the end. The trajectory schema and mask decide what the gradient blames.

next.note: Give the loop a sandbox with timeout and retry semantics.
Split the loop into rollout and learner roles.

study.locator: Sections 3 to 5, arXiv:2504.20073v2: StarPO trajectory formulation, Echo Trap with reward cliffs and gradient spikes, trajectory filtering and critic stabilization

study.title: From-scratch agentic training system
study.locator: Sections 19.10.4 to 19.10.8: `SandboxEnv` with subprocess plus timeout, `Policy` with per-token ratio plus clip plus KL, `RolloutWorker` chaining generate to execute to observe, `GRPOAgentTrainer` with group advantage and turn-only loss on Qwen2.5-0.5B (page read 2026-10-14)
study.depth: Runs on CPU as written under 500 lines. Read the production-gap table for vLLM, FSDP and Ray, but do not build them here.

focus: State holds the prompt plus history. Actions are model tokens. Observations are tool outputs the policy does not control.
The loss covers action tokens only. Training on observation tokens teaches the model to predict tool content.
One terminal reward grades the whole trajectory. Credit assignment decides which turns the gradient moves.
Bound turns with `max_turns` and a finish action. Unbounded loops hang on the first bad tool call.
units.reproduce: From a blank file, define a 2-turn tool trajectory with prompt, turn contexts, action tokens, one tool observation and a final reward. Mark exactly which tokens enter the loss and show that an unmasked observation term trains the model to emit tool text.
traps: Averaging the loss over observation tokens. Mask them before any mean.
Treating a tool error string as a policy mistake. It is an observation; the mistake is the action that caused it.
Ending the episode on timeout without recording it. Timeouts are terminal data, not missing data.

selfTest.q: Which tokens enter the loss in a tool trajectory?
selfTest.a: Model-generated action tokens only. Prompt and tool observations condition later turns but carry no loss.

selfTest.q: Why is the tool state only partially observed?
selfTest.a: The model sees history plus tool outputs, not the full environment state. Hidden state must be inferred from observations.

selfTest.q: A 7-turn task fails at turn 1 but succeeds at turns 2 to 7. What does a trajectory reward do?
selfTest.a: It scores the whole trajectory once, so the good later turns share the failure unless step credit is added.

selfTest.q: What stops an agent that keeps calling tools forever?
selfTest.a: `max_turns` plus a finish action and a timeout that ends the episode with a recorded outcome.

units.title: Sandboxes, deterministic replay and tool-error, timeout and retry semantics

Replay a fixed tool trajectory deterministically from recorded seeds and tool results.
Define timeout, retry and duplicate-action rules so retried calls cannot double-count reward.
units.why: Agents run code the model wrote. Without isolation and replay rules, one bad call hangs training or corrupts results.

next.note: Place the sandbox inside the rollout worker role.
Carry retry identity into checkpoint and failure accounting.

study.title: Sandboxed code rewards in veRL
study.locator: SandboxFusion example at commit 8718ca3: code reward through a `run_code` endpoint with the prime reward manager; read the path a rollout takes from generation through reward

focus: Execute tool code in a separate process with a timeout. Never run it in the training process.
Record seeds plus tool results per turn. Replay reads the record, never re-executes.
Retries carry the same call identity. A duplicate execution must not create a second reward event.
Truncate or paginate tool outputs before they enter context. Long outputs eat the window first.
units.reproduce: From a blank file, implement `step` with `execute_code` and `finish` plus `reset`, and show that `TIMEOUT` ends the episode, unknown actions return an error observation without ending, and outputs truncate to the last 500 chars.
traps: Calling subprocess without a timeout. One infinite loop hangs the whole rollout.
Retrying a timed-out call as a new call. Side effects can run twice while the reward counts once.
Re-executing tools during replay. Nondeterministic outputs break equivalence with the recorded trajectory.

selfTest.q: Why is subprocess plus timeout not a security boundary?
selfTest.a: It limits wait time in another process but does not isolate files or network. Production needs containers or MicroVMs.

selfTest.q: A code call times out, then the retry succeeds. How many reward events is that?
selfTest.a: One, under the original call identity. The timeout observation and the retry result belong to the same attempt.

selfTest.q: What does deterministic replay need beyond the seed?
selfTest.a: Recorded tool results per turn. Re-execution can differ, so replay reads the record.

selfTest.q: Why mask tool outputs from the loss?
selfTest.a: They are environment text, not model actions. Training on them teaches the model to emit tool content.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: sandbox reset, deterministic replay with seeded tool results, and timeout, retry and duplicate-action accounting.

units.why: Decoupling rollout from training buys throughput but sells freshness. Version stamps decide whether a gradient still describes the current policy.

Measure the loop in tokens per second and update utilization.

study.locator: Behavior policy versus recorded old policy: floating point, kernels and routing make them diverge, the ratio goes wrong, and clipping cannot fix it; 70B full state about 1.22TB versus ZeRO-3 plus checkpointing about 30GB; async LlamaRL and AReaL patterns (page read 2026-10-14)

focus: The controller owns versions and dispatch. Rollout owns generation. The verifier owns scores. The learner owns weights.
Synchronous loops stamp one version per batch. Async loops mix versions, so each trajectory carries its rollout version.
Staleness is the gap between rollout weights and learner weights. Past a threshold the data is off-policy.
Engine mismatch is not staleness. Two engines can disagree on the same version, and no clip fixes that.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, draw the rollout to reward to update loop with four roles and label where the policy version is stamped, where weights sync, and where staleness enters. Then state the mismatch rule: behavior policy versus recorded old policy makes the ratio wrong, and clipping cannot fix it.
traps: Treating colocated sync as free. Broadcast and reshard still cost time and need measuring.
Calling async data on-policy. Mixed versions need importance handling or a freshness bound.
Recomputing old log probabilities from the newer policy. Old log probabilities are immutable rollout data.

selfTest.q: Which role owns the reward score?
selfTest.a: The verifier or reward worker. The learner must not recompute scores from a newer model.

selfTest.q: What changes between sync and async loops?
selfTest.a: Weight sync timing and queueing. Sync uses one version per batch; async overlaps generation with updates and mixes versions.

selfTest.q: What does a staleness threshold of 0 mean?
selfTest.a: Fully synchronous updates. Above 0 allows bounded async lag with correction.

selfTest.q: Two engines compute different log probabilities for the same version. Does PPO clipping fix the ratio?
selfTest.a: No. Clipping limits movement but cannot reconcile probabilities from different engines.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: actor, rollout, verifier and learner role separation with policy-version stamping and staleness records.
units.stopWhen: You can name each role owner from memory and your loop diagram shows version stamps, sync points and the staleness bound.

fit.note: The pinned veRL controller plus async docs and the hands-on distributed page cover roles plus staleness at explain and measure depth.

units.title: Colocated versus disaggregated generation, batching, backpressure and starvation
outcomes: Contrast colocated and disaggregated generation by memory sharing, weight sync and failure scope.
Measure batched versus single-example generation in wall time and memory on a tiny workload.
Explain backpressure and starvation with queue evidence from a rollout-update loop.
units.why: Batching and placement decide throughput. A fast generator with a full queue still starves the learner.

next.note: Add recovery and retry identity to the placed system.
Study continuous batching and KV-cache serving at depth later.

study.title: Generation throughput and queue signals
study.locator: Generation versus memory: PagedAttention with continuous batching and prefix caching, ZeRO stages with checkpointing cost, bottleneck thresholds for rollout share, sync share and communication share (page read 2026-10-14)
study.depth: Read the thresholds as diagnosis signals. Do not run multi-GPU systems here.

focus: Colocated shares GPUs and syncs fast with NCCL. Disaggregated separates resources and pays explicit transfer.
Batching is a throughput optimization, not a universal speedup. Small CPU models can gain little after padding overhead.
Backpressure means the rollout queue is full and the generator must wait. Starvation means the learner queue is empty.
Table E.1 shows the pattern: batched MATH-500 cuts 90 to 16 minutes while distillation batching gains little.
units.reproduce: Closed-book, state the 70B full-state memory sum at about 1.22TB and the reduction path through ZeRO-3 plus checkpointing to about 30GB. Then predict which side starves when tool latency dominates generation.
traps: Expecting batching to speed up every device. Padding and mask bookkeeping can erase the gain on small setups.
Sizing queues by generator speed alone. Verifier throughput and update time set the sustainable rate.
Treating disaggregation as pure win. Separate resources add transfer, scheduling and failure scope.

selfTest.q: When does colocated beat disaggregated?
selfTest.a: Small jobs with fast NCCL reshard and one failure scope. Large or tool-heavy rollouts favor separation.

selfTest.q: The rollout queue is full while the learner is busy. What is that?
selfTest.a: Backpressure on the generator. Slow or drop intake; do not grow the queue without bound.

selfTest.q: The learner queue stays empty while rollouts trickle in. What is that?
selfTest.a: Learner starvation. Generation or verification is the bottleneck, not the update.

selfTest.q: Batched evaluation cut 90 to 16 minutes but batched distillation barely moved. Why?
selfTest.a: Evaluation parallelizes independent prompts well. Distillation was already bound elsewhere, so batching added overhead without removing the bottleneck.

Deduplicate retried rollouts by call identity so one attempt counts once.
Retain every failed rollout with its reason and keep it inside budgets and metrics.

next.note: Count recovered and failed rollouts in throughput and compute.
Use the recovery record for clean reproduction.

study.title: Production gaps in fault tolerance
study.locator: Section 19.10.9 gaps table: minimal version has no fault tolerance; production needs heartbeat monitoring, auto-restart and checkpoint recovery with distributed trajectory storage (page read 2026-10-14)

focus: Checkpoint model, optimizer, sampler cursor plus RNG, and the rollout manifest together. One alone cannot resume.
Reject resume under a changed configuration. New prompts, filters or versions start a new study.
Retries share the original call identity. Deduplicate before scoring and updating.
Failed rollouts stay counted with reasons: timeout, invalid output, verifier error. Deleting them biases every rate.
units.reproduce: From a blank file, write the recovery record fields and the resume rule. Then show a retried tool call counted once under its call identity and a failed rollout retained with its reason inside the denominator of every rate.
traps: Resuming from a model checkpoint while resetting the sampler. Prompts repeat or skip silently.
Counting a retried success without its failed first attempt. Utilization and reward rates both shift.
Publishing only complete shards. Unpublished work must be verified or rebuilt before use.

selfTest.q: What must a rollout checkpoint contain?
selfTest.a: Model and optimizer state, sampler cursor plus RNG, prompt versions, rollout manifest with call identities, and config hash.

selfTest.q: The config changed after a crash. Resume or restart?
selfTest.a: Restart as a new study. Resume only under identical configuration.

selfTest.q: A call times out then succeeds on retry. How is it recorded?
selfTest.a: One attempt identity with two events: timeout observation plus final result. It counts once in every rate.

selfTest.q: Why keep failed rollouts in the manifest?
selfTest.a: Dropping them inflates success and hides verifier and timeout costs. Failures are part of the estimand.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: checkpoint and sampler recovery with retry deduplication and failed-rollout accounting.
units.stopWhen: A killed and resumed run reproduces ordered IDs exactly, a retried call counts once, and every failure carries a reason.

Measure rollout tokens per second, verifier throughput and update utilization from a tiny run.
Account total compute across sampling, inference, verification and training with failed work included.
units.why: Curricula decide which prompts teach. Throughput decides which stage binds. Both change the study if they change mid-run.

next.note: Evaluate the curriculum on held-out tasks, not on its own filter.

study.locator: Post-training loop in six stages from target definition through failure feedback; SWE-bench style task conditions with runtime limits; routing each failure back to its cause instead of discarding (page read 2026-10-14)

focus: Filter offline to prompts the starting model solves sometimes. All-correct and all-wrong groups carry no gradient.
Version prompts, filters and schedules together. A mid-run curriculum change is a new distribution.
Utilization is consumed over produced trajectories. Dropped zero-variance groups still cost tokens.
Total compute sums sampling, inference, verification and training. Failed and filtered work stays in the sum.
units.reproduce: From fixed numbers with 100 prompts, group size 4 and mean length 512, compute 400 produced rollouts and 204800 produced tokens. With 20 percent all-equal groups dropped, show 320 consumed rollouts, utilization 0.8, and state how the dropped groups change the estimand.
traps: Filtering on test prompts. The curriculum must never see held-out tasks.
Counting only consumed tokens. Produced, retried and failed tokens are real cost.
Tuning the schedule against final evaluation. Freeze the curriculum before the clean run.

selfTest.q: Why keep only prompts solved 20 to 80 percent of the time?
selfTest.a: Groups with no variance give zero advantage and no gradient. The band keeps prompts that still teach.

selfTest.q: What is update utilization?
selfTest.a: Consumed trajectories over produced trajectories. Dropped groups lower it while still costing tokens.

selfTest.q: What enters total compute?
selfTest.a: Sampling, inference, verification and training tokens plus time, including failed, retried and filtered work.

selfTest.q: A curriculum changes mid-run. What must happen?
selfTest.a: Version it as a new distribution with its own records. Do not merge its metrics with the old one.

units.practiceNote: The section mini-project covers this: prompt curriculum with filtering, rollout and verifier throughput, update utilization and total compute accounting.
units.stopWhen: Your curriculum versions every change, your utilization divides consumed by produced on the same run, and your compute sum includes failed work.

study.title: Reward-hacking probes and data flywheel
study.locator: Extended practice with reward-hacking probes through the `debug_reward_hacking` analog and the failure-to-data flywheel: route each failure back to its cause (page read 2026-10-14)

focus: Training reward cannot be the release metric. Freeze an independent harness with its own prompts, versions and judges.
Attack with hardcoded answers, length and style hacks, and leaked tests. Record which attacks score.
Judge bias (position, length, identity, self-preference) is measured with swapped-order and blinded pairs, not assumed away.
Contamination is checked with overlap probes plus perturbation sets. A no-hit report is bounded, not proof.
units.reproduce: From a blank file, plant three attacks on a fixed verifier: a hardcoded answer, a length hack, and a leaked test. Show which the verifier accepts. Then draw the over-optimization shape: training reward climbing while held-out quality peaks and declines.
traps: Hillclimbing on the public set and reporting it as generalization. Hold out tasks the curriculum never saw.
Tuning prompts until the score moves, then comparing against untuned baselines. Fix prompts across methods.
Reading a judge win rate as capability. Blind the judge, swap orders, and keep a human-reviewed sample.

selfTest.q: What is the over-optimization shape?
selfTest.a: Training reward keeps climbing while held-out quality peaks then declines. The proxy diverged from the goal.

selfTest.q: Why test on a held-out environment shift, not just held-out prompts?
selfTest.a: Specification gaming survives prompt splits when the environment stays fixed. Shifts expose hacks tied to tool or task setup.

selfTest.q: How do you audit a judge for position bias?
selfTest.a: Swap answer order on the same pairs with blinded identities and compare win rates. A biased judge follows position.

selfTest.q: An 8-gram probe finds no overlap. Is the model clean?
selfTest.a: Not proven. Probes miss paraphrases and number changes. Add perturbation sets and report the bound.

focus: Clean means a fresh checkout, fixed versions and no tuned prompts. State the seed tolerance before running.
Prespecify the extension, its baseline and the result that would falsify it. Extensions are graded on method and rigor, not on SOTA.
Keep the Qwen2.5-0.5B base fixed across SFT, IPO and RLOO. A model change is a new study.

Sweeping checkpoints and reporting the best. Fix the selection rule before evaluation.
Dropping the hacked or collapsed run. The postmortem needs its records.

selfTest.q: What counts as a clean reproduction?
selfTest.a: Fresh checkout, pinned versions, fixed prompts and decoding, score within the stated seed margin of the original.

selfTest.q: What must a prespecified extension name?
selfTest.a: The change, the baseline it must beat, the matched budget, and the result that would falsify it.

selfTest.q: The extension underperforms the baseline. What do you keep?
selfTest.a: Everything: configs, trajectories, metrics and the failed-regime analysis naming which assumption broke.
